title: ITERTL An Iterative Framework for Fine-tuning LLMs for RTL Code Generation

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The asserted first equality is algebraically false: it rewrites the negative log-likelihood as "sum_j log(P_teacher,j / log P_pi,j)". The denominator should not be log P_pi,j; in general -log P_pi,j is not equal to log(P_teacher,j / log P_pi,j). The valid cross-entropy/KL relation is E_{P_teacher}[-log P_pi] = H(P_teacher) + KL(P_teacher || P_pi), not the expression printed here. Consequently the claimed derivation of the KL objective does not follow.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.2, Equations (8)--(11), claimed theoretical analysis and EM interpretation
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text presents the update pi_{t+1}=argmax_pi E_{a~pi_t}[r_pi(s,a)] as formally showing reduced distribution mismatch and then calls it a "degenerate variant" of generalized EM. No likelihood, latent variable, E-step posterior, lower bound, or monotonicity argument is defined, so this is not an EM derivation. Moreover, even if samples were drawn from pi_t, the optimization is said to train to convergence at pi_{t+1}; the sampling distribution is therefore generally still different from the policy being optimized. Replacing pi_old with pi_t alone does not establish that mismatch or estimation error is mitigated, much less prove it.

The protocol tunes/selects on the test benchmark: models are evaluated at temperatures {0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8} and "For each test metric (pass@1, pass@5, and pass@10), the best result is chosen." This is outcome selection over multiple test-time settings, which biases the reported benchmark values upward unless the same pre-registered selection procedure is applied to every comparison. It also conflicts with the immediately preceding claim that the paper "mainly focus[es] on the pass@1 value under greedy decoding" to avoid randomness; a per-metric best-over-temperatures result is not necessarily greedy decoding.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.2, references to Table 1 and the reported benchmark comparisons
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper repeatedly relies on "Table 1" for its central numerical evidence (including the claimed 42.9%/62.2%, comparisons with RTLCoder, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4, and relative improvements), but no Table 1 or any table containing those results is present in the supplied full text. Thus the numerical comparisons cannot be checked, including which iteration/model was evaluated and whether the claimed percentage improvements are correctly calculated.

Claims such as "outperform the state-of-the-art open-source LLM," "comprehensively surpasses GPT-3.5," and "approach the level of GPT-4" are presented as established conclusions, but their sole stated evidence is the missing Table 1. In addition, the paper admits that its seven-iteration training declines after iteration five: "From the fifth to the seventh iteration, the pass@1 rate gradually decreases." It never identifies whether the headline final model/results are from iteration 5, iteration 7, or a test-selected checkpoint. The SOTA and headline-performance conclusions are therefore not reproducibly supported.

predicted_errors.error_location: Title-page metadata and reference material at the end of the paper
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The manuscript contains unreplaced ACM template placeholders and impossible publication metadata: "Proceedings of Make sure to enter the correct conference title ... Conference acronym 'XX," DOI "XXXXXXX.XXXXXXX," and "Conference acronym 'XX, June 03–05, 2018." Yet it relies on DeepSeek-Coder-Instruct-6.7B [5], LLaMA 2 [23], GPT-4, RTLCoder [12], and recent RTL benchmarks, all postdating 2018. The supplied reference list is also absent; it ends with an orphaned fragment, "summarize with human feedback. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems..." followed by unrelated received/revised dates from 2007--2009. These defects make the cited sources and claimed provenance unverifiable and the stated publication record false.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.1, definition of the training loss and quality scores
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The method says each sampled candidate is assigned a quality score using "Pyverilog and Rough-L," then optimizes a ranking loss based on those scores. However, it never defines how these two quantities are combined, their scales, whether ROUGE-L is computed against the teacher/reference code, or the identity/range of the ranking comparator r in Eq. (2). This is consequential rather than merely stylistic: the surrogate reward r_pi used throughout the claimed theory cannot be reconstructed from the stated procedure, so the experiment and the theoretical objective are not reproducible.
